Context & Objectives¶

Context

AllLife Bank is a US bank that has a growing customer base. The majority of these customers are liability customers (depositors) with varying sizes of deposits. The number of customers who are also borrowers (asset customers) is quite small, and the bank is interested in expanding this base rapidly to bring in more loan business and in the process, earn more through the interest on loans. In particular, the management wants to explore ways of converting its liability customers to personal loan customers (while retaining them as depositors).

A campaign that the bank ran last year for liability customers showed a healthy conversion rate of over 9% success. This has encouraged the retail marketing department to devise campaigns with better target marketing to increase the success ratio.

You as a Data scientist at AllLife bank have to build a model that will help the marketing department to identify the potential customers who have a higher probability of purchasing the loan.

Objective

To predict whether a liability customer will buy personal loans, to understand which customer attributes are most significant in driving purchases, and identify which segment of customers to target more.

Data Dictionary¶

  • ID: Customer ID
  • Age: Customer’s age in completed years
  • Experience: #years of professional experience
  • Income: Annual income of the customer (in thousand dollars)
  • ZIP Code: Home Address ZIP code.
  • Family: the Family size of the customer
  • CCAvg: Average spending on credit cards per month (in thousand dollars)
  • Education: Education Level. 1: Undergrad; 2: Graduate;3: Advanced/Professional
  • Mortgage: Value of house mortgage if any. (in thousand dollars)
  • Personal_Loan: Did this customer accept the personal loan offered in the last campaign? (0: No, 1: Yes)
  • Securities_Account: Does the customer have securities account with the bank? (0: No, 1: Yes)
  • CD_Account: Does the customer have a certificate of deposit (CD) account with the bank? (0: No, 1: Yes)
  • Online: Do customers use internet banking facilities? (0: No, 1: Yes)
  • CreditCard: Does the customer use a credit card issued by any other Bank (excluding All life Bank)? (0: No, 1: Yes)

Data Preprocessing¶

Treating 'Experience' Values¶

In [218]:
# uncovering negative values in the 'experience' column
data[data["Experience"] < 0]["Experience"].unique()
Out[218]:
array([-1, -2, -3])
In [219]:
# filtering the DataFrame to select rows where "Experience" column is less than 0
negative_experience_count = (data["Experience"] < 0).sum()

# displaying the results
print(f"Total values less than 0 in 'Experience' column: {negative_experience_count}")

Total values less than 0 in 'Experience' column: 52

As observed in the statistical summary, we seem to have obtained a confirmation that there are in fact 52 unique negative values under the 'Experience' column. Because there's no real world scenario where that's applicable, we'll be assuming that it's the result of a data input error and proceed to correct it.

In [220]:
# Correcting negative values in the 'experience' columns
data["Experience"].replace(-1, 1, inplace=True)
data["Experience"].replace(-2, 2, inplace=True)
data["Experience"].replace(-3, 3, inplace=True)
In [221]:
# confirming that data processing was successfully conducted
negative_experience_count = (data["Experience"] < 0).sum()
print(f"Total values less than 0 in 'Experience' column: {negative_experience_count}")

Total values less than 0 in 'Experience' column: 0

Mapping 'Education' Values¶

In [222]:
# mapping 'Education' values 1=Undergrad, 2=Graduate, 3=Advanced/Professional

data["Education"].replace(2, "Graduate", inplace=True)
data["Education"].replace(3, "Professional", inplace=True)

In [233]:
# defining a function to help categorize CCAvg into groups
def categorize_ccavg(CCAvg):
    if CCAvg < 0 or CCAvg > 10:
        return 'Outside Range'
    elif 0 <= CCAvg < 1:
        return '<1k'
    elif 1 <= CCAvg < 2:
        return '<2k'
    elif 2 <= CCAvg < 3:
        return '<3k'
    elif 3 <= CCAvg < 4:
        return '<4k'
    elif 4 <= CCAvg < 5:
        return '<5k'
    elif 5 <= CCAvg < 6:
        return '<6k'
    else:
        return 'Above 6k' #setting values above 6k as its own group given it being marked as an outlier in the above boxplot

# applying the categorization function to CCAvg column
df['CCAvgGroup'] = df['CCAvg'].apply(categorize_ccavg)

# converting 'CCAvgGroup' to an ordered categorical type with a defined order
categories_order = ['<1k', '<2k', '<3k', '<4k', '<5k', '<6k', 'Above 6k']
df['CCAvgGroup'] = pd.Categorical(df['CCAvgGroup'], categories=categories_order, ordered=True)

# customer count for each group
ccavg_count = df.groupby('CCAvgGroup')['ID'].count().reset_index(name='CustomerCount')

print(ccavg_count)

# adding a line break
print()

# introducing a bar plot to visualize distribution
plt.figure(figsize=(12, 6))
sns.barplot(x='CCAvgGroup', y='CustomerCount', data=ccavg_count, palette='viridis')
plt.title('Customer Count per CCAvg Group')
plt.xlabel('CCAvg Group')
plt.ylabel('Customer Count')

plt.show()

  CCAvgGroup  CustomerCount
0        <1k           1683
1        <2k           1376
2        <3k           1039
3        <4k            319
4        <5k            219
5        <6k             97
6   Above 6k            267
  • We've proceeded to segment the customer count to help us see the distribution when grouping customers by spending behaviors
  • Observed outliers were segmented into its own group labeled as 'Above 6k'
  • Based on the above criteria, we can observe that the majority of customers (81%) seem to be spending less than 3000 dollars per month on credit cards with 1683 customers (33%) spending less than 1000 dollars per month.

def distribution_plot_wrt_target(data, predictor, target):
    """
    Print the category counts and plot a stacked bar chart

    data: dataframe
    predictor: independent variable
    target: target variable
    """
    fig, axs = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(12, 10))

    target_uniq = data[target].unique()

    axs[0, 0].set_title("Distribution of target for target=" + str(target_uniq[0]))
    sns.histplot(
        data=data[data[target] == target_uniq[0]],
        x=predictor,
        kde=True,
        ax=axs[0, 0],
        color="teal",
        stat="density",
    )

    axs[0, 1].set_title("Distribution of target for target=" + str(target_uniq[1]))
    sns.histplot(
        data=data[data[target] == target_uniq[1]],
        x=predictor,
        kde=True,
        ax=axs[0, 1],
        color="orange",
        stat="density",
    )

    axs[1, 0].set_title("Boxplot w.r.t target")
    sns.boxplot(data=data, x=target, y=predictor, ax=axs[1, 0], palette="gist_rainbow")

    axs[1, 1].set_title("Boxplot (without outliers) w.r.t target")
    sns.boxplot(
        data=data,
        x=target,
        y=predictor,
        ax=axs[1, 1],
        showfliers=False,
        palette="gist_rainbow",
    )

    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()
In [242]:
def stacked_barplot(data, predictor, target):
    """
    Print the category counts and plot a stacked bar chart

    data: dataframe
    predictor: independent variable
    target: target variable
    """
    count = data[predictor].nunique()
    sorter = data[target].value_counts().index[-1]
    tab1 = pd.crosstab(data[predictor], data[target], margins=True).sort_values(
        by=sorter, ascending=False
    )
    print(tab1)
    print("-" * 120)
    tab = pd.crosstab(data[predictor], data[target], normalize="index").sort_values(
        by=sorter, ascending=False
    )
    tab.plot(kind="bar", stacked=True, figsize=(count + 5, 5))
    plt.legend(
        loc="lower left", frameon=False,
    )
    plt.legend(loc="upper left", bbox_to_anchor=(1, 1))
    plt.show()

Model Building¶

Model Evaluation Criterion¶

Potential Wrong Prediction

  • Predicting a customer will take a loan when in reality, they won't (FP)
  • Predicting a customer will not take a loan, when in reality they will (FN)

What Scenario is most relevant to the business?

  • If we predict that a customer will take a loan when in reality they won't, then company will have to bear the costs associated with lack of return on investment on the marketing campaign
  • If we predict that a customer will not take a loan when in reality they would, then the company would have suffered the loss of a conversion opportunity and a potential revenue stream

Conclusion: Loosing a potential revenue stream is more costly to the company than the cost associated with the lack of return on investment in a marketing campaign.

How can we reduce the impact?

We want the recall to be maximized. The greater the recall score, the higher are the chances of minimizing False Negatives.

Building Decision Tree 0)¶

In [261]:
def model_performance_classification_sklearn(model, predictors, target):
    """
    Function to compute different metrics to check classification model performance

    model: classifier
    predictors: independent variables
    target: dependent variable
    """

    # predicting using the independent variables
    pred = model.predict(predictors)

    acc = accuracy_score(target, pred)  # to compute Accuracy
    recall = recall_score(target, pred)  # to compute Recall
    precision = precision_score(target, pred)  # to compute Precision
    f1 = f1_score(target, pred)  # to compute F1-score
    print(classification_report(target,pred))

    # creating a dataframe of metrics
    df_perf = pd.DataFrame(
        {"Accuracy": acc, "Recall": recall, "Precision": precision, "F1": f1,},
        index=[0],
    )
    return df_perf
In [262]:
def confusion_matrix_sklearn(model, predictors, target):
    """
    To plot the confusion_matrix with percentages

    model: classifier
    predictors: independent variables
    target: dependent variable
    """
    y_pred = model.predict(predictors)
    cm = confusion_matrix(target, y_pred)
    labels = np.asarray(
        [
            ["{0:0.0f}".format(item) + "\n{0:.2%}".format(item / cm.flatten().sum())]
            for item in cm.flatten()
        ]
    ).reshape(2, 2)

    plt.figure(figsize=(6, 4))
    sns.heatmap(cm, annot=labels, fmt="")
    plt.ylabel("True label")
    plt.xlabel("Predicted label")
    plt.show()

We will build our model using DecisionTreeClassifier function, while using default 'gini' criteria to split. In theory, one could use entropy as an alternative approach to split - however given the observed outliers in our dataset, we're opting to go for an impurity measure with more robustness to outliers.

Max Depth Pruning¶

Building Decision Tree 1)¶

DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=3, random_state=1)

Setting a max_depth of 3 as a pre-pruning method to bound hyperparameters and limit the depth at which our decision tree can grow. As we know, the more depth a decision trees reaches, the higher the likelihood for overfitting.

Post-Pruning¶

Cost Complexity Pruning¶

In [290]:
clf = DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=1)
path = clf.cost_complexity_pruning_path(X_train, y_train)
ccp_alphas, impurities = path.ccp_alphas, path.impurities

Optimizing the decision tree's complexity to enhance model accuracy and prevent overfitting by determining effective alpha values for pruning.

In [292]:
# plotting CCP alphas against the total impurity of leaves
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 5))
ax.plot(ccp_alphas[:-1], impurities[:-1], marker="o", drawstyle="steps-post")
ax.set_xlabel("effective alpha")
ax.set_ylabel("total impurity of leaves")
ax.set_title("Total Impurity vs effective alpha for training set")
plt.show()

  • As alpha increases (more regularization), the complexity of the model decreases. This is because higher regularization penalizes complex models, leading to simpler models with fewer splits or smaller coefficients.

  • With decreased complexity, the model is less able to capture intricate patterns in the data. Consequently, impurity may increase because the decision boundaries become simpler, leading to more mixed classes in some nodes of the decision tree.

  • Due to the increased impurity and decreased model complexity, the accuracy of the model may decrease. This is because the simpler model might not capture all the nuances in the data, leading to poorer performance on unseen data.

In [293]:
clfs = []
for ccp_alpha in ccp_alphas:
    clf = DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=1, ccp_alpha=ccp_alpha)
    clf.fit(X_train, y_train)
    clfs.append(clf)
print(
    "Number of nodes in the last tree is: {} with ccp_alpha: {}".format(
        clfs[-1].tree_.node_count, ccp_alphas[-1]))

Number of nodes in the last tree is: 1 with ccp_alpha: 0.056364969335601575

In this case, with a ccp_alpha value of 0.056364969335601575, the resulting tree has only one node, indicating an extremely simple model. This simplicity may lead to underfitting, where the model is too basic to capture the complexities of the data, potentially resulting in lower accuracy on both training and test data.

In [294]:
clfs = clfs[:-1] #removing the last element from the list of decision tree classifiers corresponding to the highest ccp_alpha value
ccp_alphas = ccp_alphas[:-1]

node_counts = [clf.tree_.node_count for clf in clfs] #calculating the number of nodes remaining in the list clfs
depth = [clf.tree_.max_depth for clf in clfs] #calculating the max depth remaining in the list clfs
fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(10, 7))
ax[0].plot(ccp_alphas, node_counts, marker="o", drawstyle="steps-post")
ax[0].set_xlabel("alpha")
ax[0].set_ylabel("number of nodes")
ax[0].set_title("Number of nodes vs alpha")
ax[1].plot(ccp_alphas, depth, marker="o", drawstyle="steps-post")
ax[1].set_xlabel("alpha")
ax[1].set_ylabel("depth of tree")
ax[1].set_title("Depth vs alpha")
fig.tight_layout()

  • As ccp_alpha increases, the penalty for adding nodes to the tree increases. This penalty encourages the tree to be simpler, resulting in fewer nodes.

  • Similarly, as ccp_alpha increases, the penalty for increasing the depth of the tree also increases.

Accuracy vs Alpha in Training & Test Sets¶

In [295]:
train_scores = [clf.score(X_train, y_train) for clf in clfs]
test_scores = [clf.score(X_test, y_test) for clf in clfs]
In [296]:
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10,5))
ax.set_xlabel("alpha")
ax.set_ylabel("accuracy")
ax.set_title("Accuracy vs Alpha for training and test sets")
ax.plot(ccp_alphas, train_scores, marker='o', label='train', drawstyle="steps-post")
ax.plot(ccp_alphas, test_scores, marker='o', label="test", drawstyle="steps-post")
ax.legend()
plt.show()

As expected, both in training and test data we observe that as the model complexity decreases so does its accuracy. Something to consider, however based on our key problem statement, more importance needs to be place on recall.

Conclusions & Business Recommendations¶

Key Objective: To predict whether a liability customer will buy personal loans, to understand which customer attributes are most significant in driving purchases, and identify which segment of customers to target more.

Conclusions:

  • Our post-pruning model stood out as the best performing one so far, capable of successfully predicting whether a customer is the right target user for a personal loan marketing campaign with 98% accuracy, 91% recall, 93% precision and 92% F1 score.

  • Income: For individuals with income greater than 116.50 dollars and who are not undergraduates, there is a higher likelihood of taking up a loan (class 1). This suggests that higher income levels are associated with a greater propensity to take out a loan.

  • Education Level: For individuals who are not undergraduates and have an income exceeding $116.50, there is a higher likelihood of taking up a loan (class 1). This indicates that education level alone does not strongly influence the decision to take out a loan among higher income earners.

  • Family Size: Among individuals with income greater than 116.50 dollars and who are not undergraduates, those with family sizes greater than 2.50 have a higher likelihood of taking up a loan (class 1). This suggests that individuals with larger families may have greater financial needs that necessitate taking out a loan.

  • Credit Card Average (CCAvg): Among individuals with income less than or equal to 116.50 dollars, those with an average credit card spending (CCAvg) greater than 2.95 and income greater than 92.50 dollars have a higher likelihood of taking up a loan (class 1). This indicates that higher spending levels may be associated with a greater need for additional funds through a loan.

  • CD_Account (Certificate of Deposit Account): Among individuals with income less than or equal to $116.50 and CCAvg greater than 2.95, those with a CD account have a higher likelihood of taking up a loan (class 1). This suggests that individuals with certain types of financial assets may still seek additional funds through a loan.
